requirements: Reproduce the three-layer client-side scheduling stack (allocation, ordering, overload control) for black-box LLM APIs and replicate the paper's controlled evaluation across regimes, information levels, allocation alternatives, overload shedding policies, and predictor-noise sensitivity.

sub_tasks.requirements: The congestion-aware mock provider is implemented with linear per-token latency scaling and load-dependent slowdown, calibrated to match the paper's production-derived coefficients.
The mock provider module exists and exposes an interface for dispatching requests and receiving completions with simulated latencies.
Code has been implemented for a mock provider class/module (e.g., `MockProvider`) that accepts requests carrying an output-token count and returns completion events with a simulated service time.
Code has been implemented so that the mock provider tracks concurrent in-flight requests (offered load) and exposes this state to the load-dependent slowdown mechanism.

Code has been implemented so the mock provider emits per-request completion records including realized latency, arrival time, and output token count, sufficient to compute short/global P95, completion rate, deadline satisfaction, and useful goodput downstream.
Per-token linear latency scaling is implemented following the calibrated coefficients (intercept ~3294 ms, slope ~18.7 ms/token).

Code has been implemented so that under low-load (single-request, no congestion) conditions, the mock returns a service time of the form `latency_ms = intercept + slope * output_tokens` with intercept and slope taken from the calibration (defaults ≈3294 ms and ≈18.7 ms/token respectively).

Code has been implemented so the linear-latency intercept and slope are configuration parameters (not hard-coded magic numbers), enabling recalibration and the predictor-noise / sensitivity experiments described elsewhere.

In an isolated single-request unit test (no congestion), the mock's returned latency for a given output-token count matches `3294 + 18.7 * tokens` to within a small numerical tolerance (e.g., within 1% of the linear formula).
Load-dependent slowdown is implemented so per-request delay grows with concurrent load, preserving the qualitative physics that overload hurts everyone.

Code has been implemented so the effective service time for a request is scaled/multiplied by a load-dependent factor that increases monotonically with the number of concurrent in-flight requests at (or during) dispatch.
In a unit test that dispatches the same request under low vs. high concurrent load, the mock returns a strictly larger realized latency under high load, confirming load-dependent slowdown is active.

Code has been implemented so bigger jobs (larger output-token priors) incur proportionally larger absolute slowdown under congestion than smaller jobs, preserving the paper's causal chain (arrival shaping → offered load → load-dependent slowdown → completions).
The mock service physics remain fixed across policy, threshold, and predictor-noise experiments so that only client-side controls vary.

Code has been implemented so that each request's realized service scale is driven by a nominal workload field (e.g., `sim_workload_p50`) that is independent of the policy-facing p50/p90 priors used by allocation/ordering/overload.

Code has been implemented so applying multiplicative noise to policy-facing priors does not modify the mock's realized latency for a given request (predictor-noise sweep isolates client belief from server physics).
Code has been implemented so the mock provider uses seeded pseudo-random state (five reproducible seeds per regime) so that runs are deterministic given a seed.
The latency calibration measurements and coefficients from Table 1 are reproduced as configuration/reference data.

A calibration table/CSV (e.g., `paper_results/tables/latency_calibration.csv`) exists containing bucket-wise (medium/long/xlong) count, mean tokens, std tokens, mean latency (ms), and std latency (ms).
The medium bucket calibration row reports Count=3, Mean tokens≈155, Std tokens≈35, Mean latency≈4916 ms, Std latency≈608 ms (within paper-reported precision).
The long bucket calibration row reports Count=5, Mean tokens≈670, Std tokens≈259, Mean latency≈14968 ms, Std latency≈3950 ms.
The xlong bucket calibration row reports Count=10, Mean tokens≈2839, Std tokens≈907, Mean latency≈57251 ms, Std latency≈16064 ms.
A linear regression of latency (ms) on output tokens over the calibration dataset yields slope≈18.7, intercept≈3294, with R²≥0.95 (paper reports 0.97), confirming linear scaling assumed by the mock.

Workload mixes (balanced and heavy-dominated), congestion levels, token buckets, deadlines, and joint metrics (Short/Global P95, completion rate, deadline satisfaction, useful goodput) are implemented and match the paper's definitions and regime structure.
Workload mix generation supports both balanced and heavy-dominated compositions with correct per-bucket proportions.
Code has been implemented that generates a balanced workload mix with bucket proportions 50% short / 25% medium / 15% long / 10% xlong.
Code has been implemented that generates a heavy-dominated workload mix with bucket proportions 20% short / 20% medium / 30% long / 30% xlong.
The realized bucket proportions in a generated sample match the target mix within a small statistical tolerance for both mixes.
Token buckets (short, medium, long, xlong) are defined with correct output-token boundaries matching the paper's calibration.
Code has been implemented that defines four token buckets short (≤64 tokens), medium (65–256), long (257–1024), xlong (>1024) matching the ShareGPT bucket definitions used in the paper.
Each generated request is assigned a bucket label consistent with its sampled output-token count.
Two congestion levels (medium and high) are supported, controlling arrival rate / offered load so that the mock provider enters distinguishable load regimes.
Code has been implemented that parameterizes offered load with a 'medium' and a 'high' congestion setting, producing distinct arrival rates for the same workload mix.
Crossing the two mixes with the two congestion levels yields exactly four named regimes: balanced/medium, balanced/high, heavy-dominated/medium, heavy-dominated/high.
Each regime is executed with five independent random seeds per scenario as specified in the paper.
Per-request coarse token priors (p50/p90) and application deadlines are attached to each request prior to submission.
Code has been implemented that computes a coarse noisy (p50, p90) output-length prior for each generated request, correlated with the true sampled output tokens.
Code has been implemented that assigns an application deadline to each request against which deadline-satisfaction is later evaluated.
Joint metrics (Short P95, Global P95, completion rate, deadline satisfaction, useful goodput) are implemented per the paper's definitions.
Code has been implemented that computes Short P95 as the 95th-percentile latency of short-bucket requests among completed calls only.
Code has been implemented that computes Global P95 as the 95th-percentile latency over all completed requests.
Code has been implemented that computes completion rate (CR) as the fraction of submitted requests that finish successfully (not timed out / not rejected without completion).
Code has been implemented that computes deadline satisfaction as the fraction of requests that both complete and finish within their assigned deadline.
Code has been implemented that computes useful goodput as the rate (requests per second) of requests that both complete and meet their deadline, computed over the run duration/makespan.
Metric aggregation across the five seeds per regime reports mean ± standard deviation for every joint metric.
The metrics interface enforces reading tails jointly with completion so that a Short/Global P95 value produced with completion rate < 1 is reported alongside its CR rather than in isolation.
Sanity checks on measured metric values reproduce the paper's characterizations for reference workload/regime pairs.
Under balanced/high with the Final (OLC) policy, measured useful goodput is 4.2 ± 1.6 SLO-meeting requests/s (mean ± std over five seeds).
Under balanced/high and balanced/medium with the Final (OLC) policy, measured completion rate is 1.00 and deadline satisfaction is 1.00 (within reported std).
Under balanced/high with the Final (OLC) policy, measured Short P95 lies within tens of milliseconds of the quota-tiered short P95 (roughly 320–355 ms band as reported in Table 2).
The allocation layer using Deficit Round Robin with congestion-aware weight adjustment and work-conserving borrowing is implemented as described in Section 3.1.
A per-class DRR scheduler data structure and selection loop is implemented.

Code has been implemented that defines per-class queues (at minimum for a short/interactive class and a heavy class) each holding pending requests with attached coarse token priors (p50/p90 or equivalent estimated_cost).
Code has been implemented that maintains a mutable deficit counter per class, initialized to zero (or a documented starting value), and updated across selection rounds.
Code has been implemented that stores a per-class DRR weight (quantum) governing how much each class's deficit is incremented per round.

The DRR main loop visits classes in round-robin order, adds the class weight (quantum) to that class's deficit at the start of its turn, and only dispatches from that class while the deficit remains non-negative after subtracting the head request's estimated_cost.

When a class's head request has estimated_cost greater than its current deficit, the scheduler leaves that request in the queue, retains the accumulated deficit for the next round, and moves on rather than sending.

In a unit test with two classes and predetermined per-request costs, the DRR core delivers a long-run per-class dispatched-cost ratio that matches the configured weight ratio to within a small documented tolerance (e.g., within 10%).
Work-conserving borrowing allows idle classes to yield their unused send opportunities to backlogged peers.

Code has been implemented so that when the currently selected class has no eligible pending request, the scheduler does not idle but immediately advances to consider another class with backlog in the same scheduling tick.

The borrowing rule permits a backlogged class to consume send opportunities that would otherwise have gone to an empty class, so that overall dispatch does not stall while any class has pending work and provider capacity is available.

In a unit test where one class has no arrivals and the other has continuous backlog, the DRR allocator dispatches the backlogged class's requests contiguously (no idle rounds inserted for the empty class) while still respecting per-request estimated_cost against the deficit.
Congestion-aware weight adjustment biases share toward the short class as observed stress rises.

Code has been implemented that computes a congestion / stress signal for the allocator from client-observable inputs (e.g., provider load, queue pressure, tail-latency ratio, or the same severity signal used by the overload layer).
Code has been implemented that maps the congestion signal to an effective per-class weight, applied on top of the base DRR weights before deficit accumulation each round.

As the congestion signal increases, the effective weight of the short/interactive class strictly increases (or the heavy class's strictly decreases) relative to the baseline, biasing send opportunities toward latency-sensitive traffic under stress.
When the congestion signal is at its floor (no stress), the effective weights equal the baseline DRR weights, so uncongested behavior reduces to plain weighted DRR without spurious bias.
In a unit test that sweeps the congestion signal from low to high with fixed arrivals, the observed short-class share of dispatched work is monotonically non-decreasing in the congestion signal.
The allocation layer integrates cleanly with the surrounding three-layer stack.

The allocation layer's only output is the selected class for the next send opportunity; it does not choose a specific request within the class (that responsibility belongs to the ordering layer) and does not itself decide admit/defer/reject (that belongs to overload control).

Code has been implemented that exposes the allocation policy as a swappable component (e.g., an interface or config selector) so that alternatives such as Fair Queuing round-robin or Short-Priority can replace adaptive DRR without modifying the ordering or overload layers.
The 'adaptive_drr' allocation policy is selectable by name/config and is used by the 'adaptive_drr' and 'final_adrr_olc' strategies referenced in the main policy comparison.
Measured allocation-layer behavior in the main policy comparison matches the reported numbers.

Under balanced/high with the 'adaptive_drr' allocation policy (no overload control), the reproduced completion rate reaches 1.00 and deadline satisfaction reaches 1.00 (mean over five seeds), matching the values in Table 2 within seed noise.
Under balanced/high with 'adaptive_drr' alone, the reproduced short-request P95 is approximately 349 ms (mean over five seeds), within a documented tolerance around the reported 349.3±36.2 ms.

Under heavy-dominated/high with 'adaptive_drr' alone, the reproduced completion rate is approximately 1.00 (matching 1.00±0.01 in Table 2) and useful goodput is approximately 2.3 SLO-meeting requests/s within seed noise.
The intra-class ordering layer using slowdown-aware feasible-set scoring (wait/cost, size/ref, urgency) is implemented per Section 3.1.
The ordering layer module exists as a distinct component that selects a concrete request within a class from the set of feasible candidates.
Code has been implemented that defines an ordering-layer function/class that accepts a set of intra-class candidate requests and returns exactly one request to submit next.

Code has been implemented so the ordering layer is invoked only after the allocation layer selects a class and before the overload control layer decides admit/defer/reject, matching the pipeline in Section 3.1.
Code has been implemented that operates ordering on the heavy class (i.e., ordering is applied intra-class for the heavy/long classes as described in Section 3.1).
The feasible-set construction restricts scoring to candidates that satisfy fairness/eligibility constraints from the allocation layer.

Code has been implemented that constructs a feasible set of candidate requests filtered by allocation-layer eligibility (e.g., class has sufficient deficit for the request's estimated cost) before scoring.
Code has been implemented that only scores and selects requests from the feasible set; ineligible candidates are excluded from ranking.
When the feasible set is empty, the ordering layer returns a null/no-selection signal so the allocation layer can move to another class rather than emitting an infeasible request.
The slowdown-aware scoring function score = w1*(wait/cost) - w2*(size/ref) + w3*urgency is implemented per Section 3.1.
Code has been implemented that computes the wait/cost term where `wait` is the request's queue residence time (current_time minus enqueue_time) and `cost` is the token-prior estimate for the request.
Code has been implemented that computes the size/ref term where `size` is the token-prior estimate and `ref` is a reference size normalizer, and this term is subtracted (favoring smaller jobs).
Code has been implemented that computes an `urgency` term capturing deadline proximity (e.g., inverse or monotonic function of remaining time to deadline) and adds it to the score.
Code has been implemented that combines the three terms with configurable non-negative weights w1, w2, w3 forming `score = w1*(wait/cost) - w2*(size/ref) + w3*urgency`.
Code has been implemented that guards against division-by-zero and non-finite values in the wait/cost and size/ref terms (e.g., epsilon floor on cost and ref) so scoring never produces NaN/Inf.
Ordering selection behavior follows the scoring rule: older, smaller, more-urgent feasible jobs are preferred.
In a unit test with two otherwise identical feasible candidates differing only in wait time, the ordering layer selects the older request.
In a unit test with two feasible candidates of identical age and urgency but different cost/size priors, the ordering layer prefers the smaller (lower-cost) request.
In a unit test with two feasible candidates identical in wait and cost but different in deadline proximity, the ordering layer prefers the more-urgent request.
The ordering layer implements deterministic tie-breaking (e.g., by request enqueue id) so that identical scores produce a stable, reproducible selection across runs with the same seed.
Ordering-layer feasibility constraints are respected across all experimental runs.
Code has been implemented that records/asserts whenever the ordering layer would emit a request outside the feasible set, so violations can be counted at run end.
Across all reported runs the total number of ordering-layer feasibility violations is zero, matching the paper's statement that zero violations were observed.
The overload controller with severity score, thresholds t1=0.45/t2=0.65/t3=0.80, and cost-ladder bucket policy (medium=0, long=1, xlong=2, short never rejected) is implemented per Section 3.1.
The overload controller module exists and is invoked at the admission boundary before requests are dispatched to the mock provider.

Code has been implemented that defines an OverloadController class/module (or equivalent) exposing an admission decision function returning one of {admit, defer, reject} for each pending request prior to dispatch.

Code has been implemented that integrates the overload controller after the allocation and ordering layers so it can block or delay the concrete request the ordering layer selects, per the layered data path in Figure 1.
The severity score is computed as a weighted combination of provider load, queue pressure, and tail latency ratio.
Code has been implemented that computes severity = w_load * provider_load + w_queue * queue_pressure + w_tail * tail_latency_ratio, combining three observable signals into a single scalar.
Code has been implemented that maintains a rolling estimate of provider_load (e.g., from recent completion latencies) that updates as new completions are observed through the API.
Code has been implemented that computes queue_pressure from outstanding in-flight work (e.g., number or estimated token cost of pending/in-flight requests) at the time of each admission decision.
Code has been implemented that computes tail_latency_ratio from a recent-window tail statistic (e.g., recent P95 or P90 completion latency normalized to a baseline) rather than instantaneous latency.

When provider_load, queue_pressure, and tail_latency_ratio are all near their nominal low values, the computed severity is below the defer threshold t1=0.45 and the controller admits requests unconditionally.
The three progressive severity thresholds t1=0.45 (defer), t2=0.65 (reject-xlong), and t3=0.80 (reject-long) are applied in order.
Code has been implemented that defines the defer threshold t1 = 0.45, reject-xlong threshold t2 = 0.65, and reject-long threshold t3 = 0.80 as configurable parameters with those exact default values.
For severity below t1=0.45, the controller admits all requests regardless of bucket (no defer/reject actions triggered).
For severity in [t1, t2) i.e., [0.45, 0.65), the controller triggers defer actions for non-short buckets according to the cost ladder without issuing rejects at this severity band.
For severity in [t2, t3) i.e., [0.65, 0.80), the controller rejects xlong requests while long requests remain in defer (not reject) status at this severity band.
For severity at or above t3=0.80, the controller rejects both long and xlong requests.
The cost-ladder bucket policy maps buckets to severity weights medium=0, long=1, xlong=2 and never rejects short requests.
Code has been implemented that defines a bucket_policy named 'ladder' (or equivalent 'cost ladder') mapping bucket labels to numeric weights: medium -> 0, long -> 1, xlong -> 2.

Code has been implemented that ensures short-bucket requests are never rejected by the overload controller under any severity value (short is excluded from the reject decision path regardless of severity).
Code has been implemented that ensures medium-bucket requests (bucket weight 0) are admitted without defer or reject actions under the default cost-ladder policy (medium sees no shedding).

Code has been implemented that uses the bucket weight in combination with the severity level to determine whether a non-short request enters defer or reject state (larger bucket weight -> shed earlier as severity rises).
The controller supports pluggable alternative bucket policies for the §4.6 comparison (ladder, uniform mild, uniform harsh, reverse).
Code has been implemented that exposes the bucket_policy as a selectable configuration knob accepting at least the values 'ladder' (default), 'uniform_mild', 'uniform_harsh', and 'reverse'.
Code has been implemented such that the 'uniform_mild' bucket policy applies one shared mid-tier severity weight to medium/long/xlong (class-agnostic among non-short work) while short remains exempt.
Code has been implemented such that the 'uniform_harsh' bucket policy applies the harshest non-short tier uniformly to medium/long/xlong.
Code has been implemented such that the 'reverse' bucket policy inverts the long/xlong ordering relative to the cost ladder (long weighted more heavily than xlong) as a stress contrast.
Overload actions are recorded and yield the expected behavior in main-benchmark runs: short receives zero rejects, and rejections concentrate on xlong.
Code has been implemented that logs per-request overload actions (admit, defer, reject) tagged by bucket so aggregate counts per bucket can be produced (as summarized in Figure 5).
When aggregating Final (OLC) main-benchmark runs (four regimes x five seeds = 20 runs) under the default cost-ladder policy, the total number of short-bucket rejections is exactly 0.

When aggregating Final (OLC) main-benchmark runs under the default cost-ladder policy, the majority of reject actions fall on the xlong bucket (xlong reject count exceeds long reject count and exceeds medium reject count).
When aggregating Final (OLC) main-benchmark runs under the default cost-ladder policy, medium-bucket requests show zero reject and zero defer actions (medium is admitted through, per §4.7).
Under the default cost-ladder policy, controller behavior matches reported per-run defer/reject counts on balanced/high and heavy/high.
Under balanced/high with the default cost-ladder policy and Final (OLC) stack, the mean number of reject actions per run (five seeds) is approximately 4.8 (Table 5).
Under balanced/high with the default cost-ladder policy and Final (OLC) stack, the mean number of defer actions per run (five seeds) is approximately 8.6 (Table 5).
Under heavy-dominated/high with the default cost-ladder policy and Final (OLC) stack, the mean number of reject actions per run (five seeds) is approximately 14.0 (Table 5).
Under heavy-dominated/high with the default cost-ladder policy and Final (OLC) stack, the mean number of defer actions per run (five seeds) is approximately 20.0 (Table 5).
The ShareGPT-derived trace replay validates the qualitative ordering of policies with reported improvements matching Table 2 (real-trace).
The ShareGPT trace ingestion and bucket distribution setup is implemented to produce the reported real-world token bucket mix.
Code has been implemented to load or synthesize a ShareGPT-English derived output-token distribution containing 388,246 assistant responses drawn from ~50k conversations.
Code has been implemented to classify each ShareGPT response into token buckets using thresholds: short (≤64 tokens), medium (65–256), long (257–1024), xlong (>1024).
The measured ShareGPT bucket distribution matches the reported split: 12% short, 42% medium, 46% long, and <1% xlong.

Code has been implemented to feed the ShareGPT-derived bucket distribution as the workload generator input to the mock provider, replacing the synthetic balanced (50/25/15/10) and heavy-dominated (20/20/30/30) mixes.
The three compared strategies (direct_naive, quota_tiered, final_adrr_olc) run on the ShareGPT trace under high congestion with proper seeding and metric collection.
Code has been implemented to execute direct_naive, quota_tiered, and final_adrr_olc policies on the ShareGPT replay under the high-congestion regime with multiple seeds for mean±std reporting.
Code has been implemented to compute short-P95 latency, global-P95 latency, makespan, and deadline satisfaction per run and aggregate as mean±std over seeds for the ShareGPT replay.
Code has been implemented to emit a results table matching the structure of Table 2 (real-trace) with columns Strategy, Short P95 (ms), Global P95 (ms), Makespan (ms), Satisfaction.
Numerical results on the ShareGPT replay match the reported Table 2 (real-trace) values within seed tolerance for each strategy.
direct_naive on ShareGPT under high congestion yields short P95 = 1449±392 ms.
direct_naive on ShareGPT under high congestion yields global P95 = 25985±1218 ms.
direct_naive on ShareGPT under high congestion yields makespan = 36352±958 ms.
direct_naive on ShareGPT under high congestion yields deadline satisfaction = 0.78±0.04.
quota_tiered on ShareGPT under high congestion yields short P95 = 324±31 ms.
quota_tiered on ShareGPT under high congestion yields global P95 = 33337±637 ms.
quota_tiered on ShareGPT under high congestion yields makespan = 41782±623 ms and satisfaction = 0.77±0.05.
final_adrr_olc on ShareGPT under high congestion yields short P95 = 330±38 ms.
final_adrr_olc on ShareGPT under high congestion yields global P95 = 17470±1342 ms (the best global-P95 across compared strategies).
final_adrr_olc on ShareGPT under high congestion yields makespan = 22001±54 ms.
final_adrr_olc on ShareGPT under high congestion yields deadline satisfaction = 0.90±0.04 (highest among the three strategies).
The qualitative claims derived from ShareGPT results (relative improvement ratios) are verified.
final_adrr_olc achieves approximately 4.4× short-P95 improvement over direct_naive on the ShareGPT trace (330 vs 1449 ms).
final_adrr_olc achieves approximately 1.9× global-P95 reduction over quota_tiered on the ShareGPT trace (17470 vs 33337 ms).
final_adrr_olc achieves approximately +15% deadline satisfaction over direct_naive on the ShareGPT trace (0.90 vs 0.78).

The qualitative ordering of policies on the ShareGPT trace (final_adrr_olc dominates on global P95 and satisfaction; quota_tiered has the lowest short P95; direct_naive has the worst short P95) matches the ordering seen on synthetic regimes.

The four-level information ladder (no-info blind, class-only, coarse, oracle) is executed across all four regimes with Final(OLC) fixed, and results match the paper's Table 3 values including the ~5.8x short P95 inflation claim.

The four information levels (no-info blind, class-only, coarse, oracle) are implemented as distinct configurations of the Final(OLC) stack, each modifying only what the client knows about per-request output length while keeping mock physics identical.

The no-information blind level is implemented such that every request is treated under a single neutral routing bucket with fixed neutral p50/p90 values; there is no per-request length estimate and no class label derived from size available to allocation, ordering, or overload.

Code has been implemented so that under no-information blind, the overload controller uses a uniform admission severity (no length-based long/xlong ladder) while still allowing deferral and rejection based on aggregate stress.

The class-only level exposes the generator's class label (short/medium/long/xlong) for routing and tiered overload decisions but keeps p50/p90 at the same neutral values used in no-information blind, so allocation weights, ordering scores, and token budgets cannot distinguish cost within a class.

The coarse (semi-clairvoyant) level uses experiment bounds to derive per-request p50/p90 priors that are consumed by allocation, ordering, and overload budgeting, matching the default configuration used elsewhere in the evaluation.
The oracle-prior level supplies each request's exact realized output-token count to the policy before dispatch, using the same sim_workload_p50 that determines mock service time.

Across all four information levels, the mock provider's per-job realized service scale is driven by the generator's nominal sim_workload_p50 field so that only what the client believes changes, not the underlying physics.

The ladder experiment sweeps all four regimes (balanced/medium, balanced/high, heavy/medium, heavy/high) crossed with the four information levels, using five independent seeds per (regime, level) cell for a total of 80 runs, with Final(OLC) held fixed as the underlying strategy.

Code has been implemented to drive the ladder experiment as a matrix over {regimes} x {information levels} x {5 seeds}, producing 80 runs total with a summary table aggregating mean and standard deviation per cell.

The Final(OLC) stack (adaptive DRR allocation + feasible-set ordering + cost-ladder overload with thresholds 0.45/0.65/0.80) is used unchanged as the underlying policy for every ladder cell, so only the information level varies across conditions.

Per-run metrics recorded include short P95 latency, global P95 latency, completion rate, deadline satisfaction, and useful goodput; these are aggregated to mean +/- std across the 5 seeds for each cell.
Results are written to paper_results/tables/prior_ablation_summary.csv with columns identifying regime, information level, and the reported metrics.

A Figure 2 equivalent plot is produced showing short-request P95 (top) and completion rate plus useful goodput (bottom) for the four information levels across the four regimes, with the no-information blind bar visually distinguished (e.g., red hatching).
Measured no-information blind results reproduce the paper's Table 3 values including the roughly 5.8x short-P95 inflation claim vs coarse priors.
No-info blind, balanced/high: short P95 matches 2067 +/- 606 ms.
No-info blind, balanced/medium: short P95 matches 1829 +/- 536 ms.
No-info blind, heavy/medium: short P95 matches 2402 +/- 556 ms with completion 0.97 +/- 0.01 and satisfaction 0.77 +/- 0.12.
No-info blind, heavy/high: completion 0.90 +/- 0.04, deadline satisfaction 0.79 +/- 0.06, and short P95 1779 +/- 468 ms are reproduced.
The ratio of no-info blind short P95 to coarse short P95 in balanced/high is approximately 5.8x (2067 / 355), matching the paper's headline inflation claim.
Under no-info blind, useful goodput remains in the ~0.8-1.9 req/s band across regimes, confirming that the blind condition is not healthy under the joint view.
Class-only measured results reproduce Table 3 values and expose the routing-without-magnitude operating point.
Class-only, balanced/high: short P95 matches 415 +/- 65 ms and useful goodput matches 5.7 +/- 1.2 req/s.
Class-only, balanced/medium: short P95 matches 428 +/- 29 ms with useful goodput 3.6 +/- 1.4 req/s and full completion/satisfaction (1.00).
Class-only, heavy/medium: completion 0.99 +/- 0.01 and satisfaction 0.85 +/- 0.13 are reproduced, distinguishing this cell from coarse (0.89/0.82) despite similar short P95.
Class-only, heavy/high: short P95 matches 352 +/- 67 ms, completion 1.00, satisfaction 0.94 +/- 0.08, and useful goodput 2.7 +/- 1.1.
Coarse (semi-clairvoyant) measured results in the ladder match Table 3 and serve as the default reference for the rest of the evaluation.
Coarse, balanced/high: short P95 matches 355 +/- 23 ms with completion 1.00, satisfaction 1.00, and useful goodput 3.9 +/- 1.6.
Coarse, balanced/medium: short P95 matches 327 +/- 9 ms, completion 1.00, satisfaction 0.997 +/- 0.008.
Coarse, heavy/medium: short P95 matches 318 +/- 11 ms with completion 0.89 +/- 0.01 and satisfaction 0.82 +/- 0.07.
Coarse, heavy/high: short P95 matches 328 +/- 13 ms, completion 1.00, satisfaction 0.93 +/- 0.06, goodput 1.8 +/- 0.9.
Oracle (upper-bound) measured results are within tolerance of Table 3 and show that oracle priors track coarse on short tails while the no-information gap remains.
Oracle, balanced/high: short P95 matches 346 +/- 33 ms with completion 1.00, satisfaction 1.00, and goodput 3.9 +/- 1.4.
Oracle, balanced/medium: short P95 matches 327 +/- 14 ms with completion 1.00 and satisfaction 1.00.
Oracle, heavy/medium: short P95 matches 327 +/- 13 ms with completion 0.94 +/- 0.04 and satisfaction 0.83 +/- 0.18.
Oracle, heavy/high: short P95 matches 344 +/- 15 ms with completion 1.00, satisfaction 0.93 +/- 0.08, and goodput 1.2 +/- 0.2.
The ladder analysis produces the interpretive contrasts the paper draws: coarse vs class-only Pareto trade-off, no-info blind as clear degradation, and oracle vs coarse near-parity on short tails.

The analysis pipeline computes and reports the class-only vs coarse short-P95 comparison in balanced/high (415 vs 355 ms) and the corresponding goodput difference (~5.7 vs ~3.9 req/s), demonstrating the throughput-vs-tail Pareto point.

The analysis pipeline reports oracle vs coarse short-P95 parity across balanced regimes (differences within tens of ms and within seed variance) and highlights that the no-information gap is not closed by moving from coarse to oracle.
Quota-tiered, adaptive DRR, and Final(OLC) policies are compared across all four regimes and results reproduce Table 4 including the 100%/100%/4.2±1.6 goodput headline under balanced/high.
The three structured policies (quota-tiered, adaptive DRR, Final OLC) and the direct-naive baseline are implemented as selectable client-side scheduling strategies.
Code has been implemented for a quota-tiered isolation strategy that enforces fixed per-class send quotas without adaptive weight adjustment or overload control.
Code has been implemented for an adaptive-DRR-only strategy that uses the DRR allocation layer and feasible-set ordering layer but disables the overload controller.
Code has been implemented for the Final (OLC) strategy that composes adaptive DRR allocation, feasible-set ordering, and the overload controller with cost-ladder shedding.
Code has been implemented for a direct-naive FIFO dispatcher used as an orientation baseline in the scatter plots.

The three allocation policies (Direct FIFO, Short-Priority, Fair Queuing) are implemented as alternative allocation-layer choices while ordering and overload control components remain fixed.
Code has been implemented for a Direct FIFO allocation policy that dispatches requests in arrival order without any class-based prioritization or round-robin logic.

Code has been implemented for a Short-Priority allocation policy that biases DRR toward the interactive/short class so short requests are served ahead of heavy requests whenever the short queue is non-empty.

Code has been implemented for a Fair Queuing allocation policy that alternates send opportunities between short and heavy classes via round-robin, giving each class equal service opportunities regardless of request size.
The Fair Queuing round-robin implementation behaves such that when both short and heavy queues are non-empty, consecutive dispatches strictly alternate between the two classes.
Swapping the allocation policy among FIFO/Short-Priority/Fair Queuing does not modify the ordering-layer scoring or the overload-control admission logic used in the run.

Predictor noise sensitivity sweep: multiplicative noise L∈{0,0.1,0.2,0.4,0.6} is applied to policy-facing p50/p90 priors across all four regimes with Final(OLC) fixed and mock physics unchanged; graceful degradation (no cliff) matches Figure 8 and per-regime bands from Section 4.10.

Code has been implemented so that the mock provider's realized per-job service scale continues to use the generator's nominal sim_workload_p50 (unperturbed) even when the policy-facing priors are noised.

Code has been implemented so that noise is applied to the priors that feed allocation weights, ordering scores (cost term), and overload budgets/cost ladder, i.e., all three layers see the perturbed values.
Code has been implemented so that at L=0 the multiplicative factor is identically 1.0 and the noise pipeline is a no-op equivalent to the coarse-priors baseline.

The Final(OLC) three-layer stack (adaptive DRR + feasible-set ordering + cost-ladder overload with thresholds t1=0.45/t2=0.65/t3=0.80) is held fixed across all noise levels and regimes.

Balanced regimes exhibit graceful, near-flat degradation under the noise sweep, matching Section 4.10's reported bands.
In balanced/high, completion rate and deadline satisfaction remain at 1.00 for every L∈{0,0.1,0.2,0.4,0.6}.
In balanced/high, useful goodput across the five noise levels stays within the reported band of roughly 3.8–4.3 SLO-meeting requests per second without a sharp cliff.
In balanced/high, short-request P95 stays in the reported band of approximately 340–352 ms across all noise levels (within seed variance).
In balanced/medium, completion rate remains 1.00 across all L values in the sweep.
In balanced/medium, short-request P95 stays near the reported 324–329 ms band across all noise levels.
In balanced/medium, useful goodput stays in the reported band of roughly 1.39–1.47 req/s across all noise levels.
Heavy-dominated regimes exhibit stronger but still graded coupling to predictor noise, matching Section 4.10's reported bands.
In heavy-dominated/high, completion rate stays near 1.0 (within measurement noise) across all L values in the sweep.
In heavy-dominated/high, short-request P95 moves from approximately 328 ms at L=0 to approximately 338 ms at L=0.6, matching the reported drift.
In heavy-dominated/high, useful goodput varies within the reported band of roughly 1.4–2.7 req/s across L∈{0,0.1,0.2,0.4,0.6} without an abrupt collapse.
In heavy-dominated/medium, completion rate spans from approximately 0.89 at L=0 up to approximately 0.94 at L=0.6, reproducing the largest completion swing observed in the sweep.
In heavy-dominated/medium, deadline satisfaction ranges within approximately 0.80–0.88 across the sweep.
Overall graceful-degradation qualitative claims across the sweep hold globally, not just per-regime.

No regime shows a discontinuous cliff in short P95, global P95, completion rate, deadline satisfaction, or useful goodput between adjacent noise levels; drift is monotonic-in-magnitude or bounded within seed variance.

The short-P95 inflation observed under noise (up to L=0.6) in every regime is substantially smaller than the multi-fold short-P95 inflation observed in §4.4's no-information-blind condition, confirming that noisy coarse priors remain far more useful than absent magnitude.
